title-group.article-title: Longitudinal patient-reported sleep disturbance during cellular therapy for lymphoma.

contrib-group.aff: Riverside University Medical Center, Chicago, IL
Central Oncology Research Hospital, Houston, TX

abstract.p: Background: Patient-reported sleep disturbance is common among patients receiving CD19-directed cellular therapy for relapsed lymphoma, but its trajectory during and after treatment is not consistently captured in routine oncology practice. We characterized longitudinal symptom burden and factors associated with clinically meaningful worsening. Methods: Participants completed the PROMIS Sleep Disturbance Short Form at baseline, day 14, day 30, and day 90 after infusion. Mixed-effects models evaluated change over time, and multivariable regression assessed baseline clinical and patient-reported predictors. A prespecified threshold was used to define clinically meaningful worsening from baseline. Results: The cohort included 143 patients. Mean symptom score was 53.9 at baseline, reached 61.5 at the period of greatest burden, and was 55.0 at the final assessment. Clinically meaningful worsening occurred in 35% of participants. In adjusted analysis, grade 2 or higher cytokine release syndrome was independently associated with worse longitudinal symptom scores (β=0.24, p=0.004). Completion rates exceeded 80% at each scheduled assessment. Conclusions: Sleep disturbance changed substantially over the treatment course among patients receiving CD19-directed cellular therapy for relapsed lymphoma. Routine longitudinal assessment may identify patients who would benefit from earlier supportive care, particularly those with grade 2 or higher cytokine release syndrome. Research Sponsor: Cell Therapy Outcomes Consortium.
